fixes.explanation: The plunder is real. Joab's men did come back with a great plunder (2 Samuel 3:22). But when Joab reaches the king, the text has him talking about Abner, not handing over the haul. Joab asks, “What have you done?”

That's right, baker. Joab says Abner “…came to deceive you and to track your movements and all that you are doing.” That's Joab's charge against Abner. Joab makes the accusation, and then he sends messengers after Abner.

No challenge shows up in the text, friend. Joab says nothing about a duel. His charge is that Abner came to deceive David and track what he was doing. Joab and his troops had come back from a raid after Abner had left, so he's telling this secondhand.

Good guess, friend, but it's not David's word. He says he and his kingdom are “…forever guiltless before the LORD…” about Abner's blood. That's the word he picks. Guiltless is what he says about himself and his kingdom.

Not the word David uses, baker. He says he and his kingdom are “…forever guiltless before the LORD concerning the blood of Abner son of Ner.” The word he picks is guiltless. Indebted never comes out of his mouth.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “…King David himself walked behind the funeral bier.” That's David, the king, walking behind Abner's bier. So this one is true.
You've got it, baker. The text says, “…all the people wept over him even more.” That comes right after David's lament for Abner. I bet it was a long, heavy day in Hebron.

The text goes another way, friend. After David's lament, it says “…all the people wept over him even more.” Going back to their homes isn't what the verse tells us. It's one of the sadder moments in the story.

That's it, baker. David takes an oath: “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!” The people urged him to eat something while it was still day. His answer was an oath.

Not what the text says, friend. The people do urge David to eat something. But David answers with an oath: “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!” That's his answer, not a meal with them.

David doesn't say a little is fine, baker. He swears, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!” That's a firm oath. He says bread or anything else.

That's the word, baker. The text says all the troops and all Israel “…were convinced that the king had no part in the murder of Abner…” Just before that, it says all the people took note and were pleased. That's how the whole crowd came to be convinced.

Good guess, baker, but it's not the word in the text. It says they were “…convinced that the king had no part in the murder…” That's a settled conclusion, not a startled reaction. The verse before it says all the people took note and were pleased.

That's right, baker. David ends with, “May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!” Right before that, he says he's weak this day and the sons of Zeruiah are too fierce for him. That request is the last thing he says in this passage.
